title: Palliative care goals and individual quality of life of patients with fibrosing lung disease and their relatives
summary:
Certain lung diseases lead to an increasing formation of scar tissue within the lungs. This connective tissue gradually replaces healthy lung tissue, resulting in a progressive decline in lung function. These diseases are referred to as “fibrosing interstitial lung diseases” (fILD).

Affected individuals frequently experience severe shortness of breath, which not only significantly limits physical capacity but also places a considerable psychological burden on patients. Over the course of the disease, many develop anxiety or depression. As lung scarring progresses, the disease cannot be cured and is, in most cases, ultimately fatal.

Although palliative care could help alleviate symptoms, improve well-being, and provide holistic support in daily life, only a few patients currently receive such assistance. When palliative measures are prescribed, this often happens very late, typically at an advanced stage of the illness. This is contrary to the wishes of many affected individuals, who would prefer to die in a familiar environment, such as at home. Nevertheless, many still pass away in the hospital and are often subjected to burdensome and aggressive medical treatments.

The aim of this study is to analyze the needs of patients and their relatives with regard to the early integration of palliative care and advance care planning. The goal is to improve quality of life and make decision-making at the end of life easier. Working with patients and their families, the study will identify individual needs and expectations concerning palliative support. The scientific approach uses various methods to gather both qualitative and quantitative insights. Based on the study results, targeted, patient-centered palliative care interventions for people with fibrosing interstitial lung diseases and their relatives can be developed and, if appropriate, integrated into care practice.
